column2: On the authority of Jābir ibn ʿAbdillāh that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, in the year of the Conquest while he was in Makkah: “Allah and His Messenger have forbidden the sale of wine, carrion, swine and idols.”
It was said: “O Messenger of Allah, what about the fat of carrion, for ships are caulked with it, hides are oiled with it, and people use it for lamps?” He said: “No,
it is unlawful.” Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “May Allah fight the Jews!
Allah forbade them the fat [of animals], so they melted it down, then sold it and consumed its price.” Recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

His words, “Allah and His Messenger have forbidden (ḥarrama)”: the verb ḥarrama is reported in the singular and in the dual, and also as “Allah has forbidden”. The dual is used in the pronoun referring to Allah and His Messenger in the hadith: “There are three things; whoever has them finds through them the sweetness of faith:

that Allah and His Messenger are more beloved to him than anything else besides them…”, to the end of the hadith (recorded by al-Bukhārī, 16, and Muslim, 67). On this basis, the singular verb ḥarrama here is understood as referring to the Messenger
ﷺ, with the forbidding attributed to Allah omitted, the implied meaning being: Allah has forbidden, and His Messenger has forbidden. It is like the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic:

“But Allah and His Messenger are more worthy that they should please Him” [al-Tawbah 9:62], that is, Allah is more worthy that they should please Him, and His Messenger is more worthy that they should please him. Similar are the poet's words:
We with what we have, and you with what you have, / are content, though opinions differ—
that is, we are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have.
Jābir (may Allah be pleased with him) made clear that he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbid these things in the year of the Conquest in Makkah.

This announcement at this time and in this place was made on the occasion of the disbelievers' entering Islam while they were engaged in these forbidden things, so he informed them that they were unlawful. This does not rule out their having been forbidden earlier.
The first of these four forbidden things is wine, which is the mother of all foul things,

because by drinking it the drinker seeks to put himself among the insane, and as a result he falls into everything unlawful, which may include assaulting those he is forbidden to marry. It brings every evil and plunges one into every affliction, which is why it is called the mother of all foul things.
The second is carrion, which may not be eaten except out of necessity to preserve life when nothing else is to be found. Excepted from this is its hide once tanned,
because this is established in the Sunnah from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (reported by al-Bukhārī, 2221, and Muslim, 366).
The third is swine, which may be neither eaten nor sold. For every animal that may not be eaten, it makes no difference whether it died of itself or was slaughtered.
The fourth is idols, which may be neither sold nor kept,
because they were made to be worshipped; rather, they must be smashed and broken. There is nothing wrong with making use of them after breaking them, in building and the like,
since they are no longer idols.

The ḥāfiẓ [Ibn Ḥajar] said in al-Fatḥ (4/425): “His words, ‘What about the fat of carrion, for ships are caulked with it, hides are oiled with it, and people use it for lamps?’, mean: is it lawful to sell it because of the benefits mentioned,

since they would make the sale valid? His words, ‘He said: No, it is unlawful’, that is, the sale. Thus some scholars, such as al-Shāfiʿī and those who followed him, explained it. Others understood his words,

‘it is unlawful’, as referring to making use of it, and said that making use of it is unlawful. This is the view of most scholars: according to them, nothing of carrion may be used at all except what has been specified by evidence, namely tanned hide.”
His words, “May Allah fight the Jews!
Allah forbade them the fat [of animals], so they melted it down, then sold it and consumed its price”: this is one of the stratagems of the Jews,

for when Allah forbade them fat, they melted it down, sold it and consumed its price. When Allah forbids something, He forbids its price; that is why the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invoked [Allah] against them.
The hadith shows that the Prophet ﷺ forbade these four things.
The Prophet ﷺ announced this prohibition in Makkah in the year of the Conquest,
so that those who had accepted Islam would hasten to refrain from these four things, both in using and in selling them.
Whatever Allah has made unlawful, selling it is unlawful and its price is unlawful.
Stratagems used to make lawful what Allah has made unlawful are forbidden.
The Jews are censured, and it is made clear that they were people who used stratagems to make the unlawful lawful.
This nation is warned against falling into such stratagems as the Jews fell into.
